talk: A liquidation preference says who gets paid first when the company is sold. With a 1x preference, investors can take their money back before anyone else gets anything. It barely matters in a big sale and matters a lot in a small one.

terms.meaning: Investors' right to get their money back first in a sale.
Investors take either their money back or their share of the sale, whichever is more.
Investors take their money back and then their share of what's left too.

questions.prompt: An investor put in $4M for 20%, with a 1x non-participating preference. The club sells for $10M. What does the investor take?
questions.hint: Compare their money back with their share of the sale.
working: Non-participating means they pick the bigger one: $4M.
whyNot: They get paid first, but only up to their preference.
$4M + $2M = $6M is participating. Non-participating means one or the other.
$2M is their 20% share. Their preference lets them take their $4M back instead.

questions.hint: The sale price minus what the investor took.
whyNot: $10M - $2M = $8M assumes the investor took their 20% share. They took their $4M back instead.

questions.prompt: Same deal, but now the club sells for $50M. What does the investor take?
questions.hint: In a big sale, which is bigger: the money back or the share?
working: $10M is bigger, so they take their share: $10M.
whyNot: $50M - $4M = $46M is what's left after a preference, not the investor's take.
$10M + $4M = $14M is participating. Non-participating gets one or the other.
In a big sale, 20% beats the money back, so they take their share.

penalty.prompt: An investor put in {inv} for {share}, with a 1x non-participating preference. The club sells for {sale}. What does the investor take?
penalty.hint: Money back or share of the sale, whichever is bigger.
working: Share of the sale: {sale} x {share} = {sale * share|usd}.
They take the bigger one: {max(inv, sale * share)|usd}.

traps.why: That's participating. Non-participating takes one or the other.
They take the bigger of the two, not the smaller.

call.title: Two term sheets
call.prompt: Both investors offer $5M to build a new stand, worth about 1,500 more fans a match. The first values the club at $20M pre-money with a 1x non-participating preference. The second values it at $25M pre-money but wants a 2x participating preference. You expect to sell the club for about $40M one day.

options.label: $20M pre-money, 1x non-participating
options.result: Good call. $20M + $5M = $25M post-money, so they own $5M / $25M = 20%. At a $40M sale they take $40M x 20% = $8M, leaving $40M - $8M = $32M for everyone else.

options.label: $25M pre-money, 2x participating
options.result: The headline is higher, but $25M + $5M = $30M post-money and at a $40M sale they take 2 x $5M = $10M first, then $5M / $30M = about 16.7% of the rest: ($40M - $10M) x 16.7% = about $5M. $10M + $5M = $15M to them, leaving $40M - $15M = $25M. The bigger valuation cost everyone else $32M - $25M = $7M.

options.label: Take neither
options.result: No deal, no stand. The money would have added 1,500 x $18 = $27,000 a matchday.

takeaway: Terms can matter more than the valuation. Always ask: who gets paid first, and how much?
